I generalise the simplex construction to a union of layers {x ≥ 0 : Σx ∈ S}, with exact closed-form counts of |A+A| and |A−A| for every layer subset S. Keep the exact simplex search to pick (d, n). Then run an incremental hill-climbing local search that toggles lattice points from the radius-(n+1) simplex pool, using dict-based sum/difference counts. The best set found is returned, with the plain simplex as the fallback.

Keep the exact simplex search as the baseline, then hill-climb over weighted simplices {x≥0 : Σ wᵢxᵢ ≤ T} with integer weights. Each candidate is embedded into the integers and scored exactly with numpy; the best one is returned, and the plain simplex stays as the fallback.

I added a second family, 0/1 vectors of Hamming weight ≤ n embedded in base 3, with exact closed-form counts of |A+A| and |A−A|. The search takes whichever of this family or the simplex scores best by formula. I haven't run it, so I don't know yet whether it beats the simplex.

Generalise the simplex to a coordinate-capped simplex {x≥0, Σx≤n, xᵢ≤m}. Candidates near the best simplex dimension, including large simplices cut down to ≤4000 points, are scored exactly with numpy using chunked unique counts. The best-scoring set is returned, with the plain simplex as the fallback

Build A as the lattice points of a d-dimensional simplex {x ≥ 0, Σx ≤ n}, embedded into the integers in base 2n+1. It picks (d, n) by exact combinatorial counts of |A+A| and |A−A| under the size and magnitude limits, and does no random search.

Keep the exact simplex search as a fallback, then try random congruence-coset subsets of larger simplices: points with Σcᵢxᵢ ≡ r (mod p), embedded in base 2n+1.
